My story · Colombia to the world

From Paipa, Boyacá, to the stars.

I was born in Paipa, Boyacá, Colombia. My route into astronomy began at UPTC, where I became the first Physics graduate with an astronomy-focused thesis and helped co-found the Astronomy and Cosmology group. Graduate study then took me to the United States for my master’s degree and to Australia for my Ph.D. at ANU.

I was born in Paipa, Boyacá, Colombia. My journey into astronomy began with studying Physics and finding a way to turn my curiosity about the Universe into research.

At the Universidad Pedagógica y Tecnológica de Colombia (UPTC), I became the first student to earn a Physics degree with a thesis focused on Astronomy. I then helped co-found UPTC’s Astronomy and Cosmology group, helping create a place where other students could explore astronomy, too.

Leaving Paipa to study physics, and then continuing from Colombia to the United States and Australia, changed the scale of the questions I could pursue—but not the reason I was drawn to science: curiosity about how the Universe works. At UPTC, I also saw how much it matters for students to find a community where astronomy is taken seriously. Helping establish the Astronomy and Cosmology group was one way to make that space for others. Today, I bring together observational research, open-source methods, and outreach because I want both to advance our understanding of young planetary systems and to help more people imagine themselves taking part in science.

01 / About

Observational astronomy, from young stars to forming planetary systems.

I investigate how young stellar systems evolve by combining millimeter interferometry with optical and infrared spectroscopy. My work connects disk structure and chemistry with accretion, outflows, and the properties of young stars and brown dwarfs.

How I work

I bring together observations from facilities including ALMA and JWST with optical and near-infrared spectroscopy, data reduction, and physical interpretation. I also develop reproducible Python tools for extracting stellar properties from complex spectra.

ALMA interferometryOptical & NIR spectroscopyYoung stellar objectsAccretion & outflowsProtoplanetary disksScientific Python

Research in practice

My experience spans interferometric imaging, spectral classification, extinction and veiling analysis, and collaborative observing programs. I value methods that are physically grounded, reproducible, and useful to the wider research community.

The path that brought me here

From Paipa, Boyacá, to the international astronomy community

I was born in Paipa, Boyacá, Colombia. At the Universidad Pedagógica y Tecnológica de Colombia (UPTC), I became the first student to earn a Physics degree with an astronomy-focused thesis and helped co-found the university’s Astronomy and Cosmology group. That experience helped me see how much it matters to create opportunities for astronomy where they are not yet well established.

My studies then took me to the United States for graduate education and to Australia, where I completed my Ph.D. in Astrophysics at the Australian National University in 2018. Those experiences broadened my scientific horizons while keeping me connected to the place where my journey began.

That connection also shapes my outreach. Through “If I can do it, you can do it,” I visit schools in remote communities to share science with children and encourage them to imagine their own futures in science. I see this as a way to pass forward the sense of possibility that helped shape my own path.

A DISTINCTIVE DISCOVERY · 2022

A young brown dwarf with quasi-spherical mass loss

As part of the ODISEA survey with ALMA, I helped identify an unusual CO shell associated with a likely young brown dwarf in Ophiuchus. The result reported the first evidence of quasi-spherical mass loss in a young brown dwarf, revealing an unexpected phenomenon in the early evolution of substellar objects.

ODISEAALMAKMOSBrown dwarfsMass loss

Read the NRAO story: “The Mouse That Roared” ↗  ·  Read the peer-reviewed paper in The Astrophysical Journal ↗

03 / Open-source tools

Building tools for young-star spectroscopy.

Alongside observing and interpreting young stellar objects, I develop Python tools to make their spectral characterization more physically appropriate and reproducible.

Python · Spectral classification · Open source

YSOFit — characterizing young, embedded, and accreting stars

I developed YSOFit, a Python workflow for deriving spectral types (SpT), visual extinctions (AV), and continuum veiling (rλ) for young, low-mass stars and brown dwarfs from optical and near-infrared spectra. The publicly available GitHub repository is named YSOType.

Many classification tools use empirical field-dwarf templates that do not capture the low-gravity features of pre-main-sequence objects. They may also be limited to optical wavelengths or assume spectra are unreddened and unveiled. This workflow is designed to address those limitations.

550–2500 nmLow-gravity templatesOptical + NIRStars + brown dwarfs

How the workflow works

  1. Match the templates. Use low-gravity synthetic spectra spanning 550–2500 nm, matched to each observed spectrum’s resolution.
  2. Measure veiling independently. Estimate the dilution of photospheric features before fitting extinction, and report veiling separately in the optical, J, H, and K bands.
  3. Fit spectral type and extinction. Keep the measured veiling fixed, then evaluate uncertainties from the SpT–extinction degeneracy, veiling, and the extinction law.

Each spectrum is processed individually, and each solution is checked interactively—so the final classification is not treated as a blind automated result.

05 / Experience

A career built around collaborative astronomy.

My path has connected research, observatory science, and the development of astronomy communities.

What I bring to a team

I bring experience connecting observational data, physical interpretation, and practical analysis workflows: interferometric imaging, molecular-line studies, optical/NIR spectroscopy, Python development, and collaborative survey science. I also value mentoring and building scientific communities.

Open to new opportunities

I welcome conversations about research scientist, observatory / ALMA support, and faculty positions where my expertise in interferometry, star formation, spectroscopy, and scientific software can contribute.

06 / Education & outreach

“If I can do it, you can do it.”

Science belongs to everyone. I bring astronomy and scientific curiosity into direct conversation with children—and help connect the people and places behind modern astronomy with wider audiences.

Science outreach · Colombia

Big questions belong to every child.

Through “If I can do it, you can do it,” I visit schools in remote communities and share science with girls and boys. I want children to feel welcome asking questions about the natural world, space, and the Universe—and to imagine themselves as people who can do science.

For me, outreach is personal: access to opportunity can change the path a young person believes is possible.

Remote schoolsScience educationGirls and boys in STEM
Science communication · ALMA Ambassador

Connecting people with the science behind the observatory.

As an ALMA Ambassador, I helped communicate the science and people behind one of the world’s leading radio observatories. Astronomy is built through collaboration, shared expertise, and public curiosity—not only through the data we collect.

This role connects naturally with my outreach work: making the science of star and planet formation understandable and inviting more people into the conversation.

ALMAPublic engagementCollaborative astronomy
Research recognition · 2018

The Gruber Fellowship: international recognition of my research

In 2018, I received the Gruber Cosmology Fellowship, becoming the first Colombian woman to receive this distinction. The fellowship was a meaningful milestone in my journey from Paipa, Boyacá, to the international astronomy community.

This recognition is part of my story—not only as a researcher, but as someone who hopes that young people in Colombia can see a place for themselves in science.
